title: Karnataka Collects Over 45 Lakh Litres of Used Cooking Oil as State Intensifies Trans Fat Crackdown
excerpt: The state's food safety administration has ramped up enforcement under FSSAI's RUCO initiative, directing oil manufacturers, hotels, and bakeries to strengthen compliance with trans fat reduction norms.
body:
Karnataka's Food Safety and Drug Administration has escalated its campaign against trans fats in the food supply chain, with the state now reporting the collection of over 45 lakh litres of used cooking oil since 2024 under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India's RUCO (Repurpose Used Cooking Oil) initiative, according to The Hindu.

The figure marks a significant jump from the 32.68 lakh litres collected during financial years 2024-25 and 2025-26, as reported at a state-wide review meeting last July. The accelerating pace of collection reflects both tightening enforcement and growing participation from food business operators across the state.

Mandatory Fortification and Testing

In directives issued during a recent review meeting chaired by the Commissioner of Food Safety and Drug Administration in Bengaluru, all cooking oil manufacturers in Karnataka have been ordered to fortify their products with Vitamins A and D, maintain strict hygiene standards during production, and ensure proper labelling in line with FSSAI norms.

Manufacturers have also been directed to get their oils tested at least once every six months, with compliance now being actively monitored. The move targets the quality of oil at the production stage, before it reaches kitchens and commercial establishments.

Health Risks Drive Enforcement

The crackdown comes amid growing medical evidence linking trans fats in reused cooking oil to non-communicable diseases. Dr. Vishal Rao, an oncologist and head and neck surgeon at HCG Cancer Centre, has been among the medical professionals advising the state on this initiative. He has highlighted the direct connection between trans fat consumption and elevated risks of heart disease and cancer, urging the food industry to adopt healthier practices.

"Vishal Rao, an oncologist and head and neck surgeon at HCG Cancer Centre, has been among the medical professionals advising the state on this initiative."

Under FSSAI rules, vegetable oil with Total Polar Compounds (TPC) exceeding 25 percent is considered unfit for human consumption. Yet a 2022 study by the Observer Research Foundation found that nearly 60 percent of used cooking oil generated in Indian cities finds its way back into the food stream, either through direct reuse in commercial kitchens or resale to unauthorized traders.

Hotels and Bakeries Under the Scanner

Karnataka's food safety authorities have issued strict instructions to hotel and bakery operators to hand over used oil to registered RUCO agencies rather than reusing it. Food Business Operators consuming more than 50 litres of oil per day are required to maintain usage records and dispose of used cooking oil only through authorized channels.

The state has also engaged the Karnataka State Bio-Diesel Development Board and RUCO agency representatives in its enforcement meetings, creating a coordinated ecosystem for collection and conversion. The collected oil is directed to authorized biodiesel manufacturing facilities, effectively converting a public health hazard into renewable fuel.

What This Means for Diaspora Kitchens

For Indians abroad, the story highlights a food safety concern that extends well beyond Karnataka. Many diaspora communities source spices, snacks, and cooking oils from India, and the trans fat content in these products has been a persistent concern. FSSAI's push for mandatory fortification and reduced trans fats in edible oils could gradually improve the quality of Indian-origin food products available internationally.

"Repeated frying of oil leads to change in physiochemical, nutritional and sensory properties of edible oil. Total Polar Compounds formed in the oil during frying have adverse effects on health."

— FSSAI directive on cooking oil safety

At home, states like Kerala have already imposed fines of up to ₹1 lakh on food business operators found violating cooking oil safety norms. FSSAI has also extended its provisional enrollment of 63 Non-Food Production units for used cooking oil collection through July 2026, signaling a longer-term commitment to scaling the RUCO ecosystem nationally.

Looking Ahead

Karnataka's accelerating oil collection numbers suggest the state is emerging as a model for RUCO implementation. The challenge remains enforcement at scale: India's vast unorganized food sector, including millions of small eateries and street vendors, largely falls outside the 50-litre-per-day threshold that triggers FSSAI's mandatory disposal rules. Expanding coverage to smaller operators and strengthening monitoring infrastructure will determine whether the state's trans fat reduction targets translate into measurable public health outcomes.
